passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: The marine biologist Baruch Rinkevich has championed an active approach to saving degraded coral reefs. Rather than wait for damaged reefs to recover on their own—a process that may take decades, if it happens at all—he proposes "gardening" them: fragments of healthy coral are grown in sheltered underwater nurseries and then transplanted onto depleted reef sites. In trials across several regions, nursery-raised fragments have survived transplantation and begun to grow, and Rinkevich argues that scaling such methods up could rebuild reef structure faster than natural recovery allows. Restoration, on his account, is a practical tool that coastal communities can use now, without waiting for distant shifts in global policy to take hold.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: The reef scientist Terry Hughes does not deny that coral gardening can restore small patches of reef, and he agrees that local nurseries have produced healthy transplants. His objection concerns scale. The world's reefs span tens of thousands of square kilometers, while even ambitious restoration projects work over a few hectares; the recent mass-bleaching events driven by ocean warming have killed corals across hundreds of kilometers in a single season. Transplanting fragments onto a reef that will bleach again the next warm summer, Hughes argues, treats the symptom rather than the cause. Worse, he warns, promoting restoration as a solution may ease the political pressure to cut the emissions that are warming the oceans in the first place.

question: Based on the texts, how would Hughes (Text 2) most likely respond to the claim presented in Text 1?

choices.text: He would deny that nursery-raised coral fragments are able to survive transplantation onto degraded reef sites, rejecting the empirical basis of Rinkevich's gardening trials outright.
He would recommend abandoning restoration projects altogether and leaving every damaged reef to recover entirely on its own, however many decades that unaided process might take.
He would grant that gardening can restore small patches yet argue it cannot match warming-driven loss and may even weaken pressure to curb emissions.
He would propose concentrating restoration on precisely those reefs judged most likely to bleach again within the next several warm summers, where transplants are most at risk.

explanation: The correct answer is C. Hughes accepts the part of Rinkevich's case that is empirical—gardening can restore small patches, and the nurseries work—so his reply is not a denial that transplants survive. His quarrel is with scale and with consequences: restoration operates over hectares while bleaching kills corals across hundreds of kilometers, so transplanting onto a reef that will bleach again treats the symptom, and promoting restoration as the answer may relieve pressure to cut emissions. C captures that concede-then-challenge stance. A denies a point Hughes grants; B pushes him to an abandon-everything position he never takes; and D recommends a targeting strategy that, on his own logic, would still lose to repeat bleaching.
